questions.prompt: What is diplomatic war in this chapter?
choices: Stopping pressure so negotiation can begin cleanly
Alternating randomly between public threats and private talk
Pressing materially while keeping a real settlement lane open

explanation.gentle: The chapter defines diplomatic war as simultaneous pressure and negotiation, not as separate phases.
explanation.direct: Begin with the structure: the operator keeps the squeeze on while preserving a credible exit.
explanation.competitive: This move turns force and settlement into one machine.

questions.prompt: Why does a face-saving exit matter so much here?
choices: Because public pressure is always unethical
Because secrecy matters more than terms
Because the other side needs a path it can accept without total humiliation

explanation.gentle: The settlement lane has to be livable enough to compete with continued resistance.
explanation.direct: Keep the acceptance test in view: an exit that reads as self-erasure will not function as leverage.
explanation.competitive: No one takes the deal if it still feels like public death.

questions.prompt: What is the main reversal attached to diplomatic war?
choices: The strategy works best when the settlement lane is vague
A fake off-ramp destroys trust and can harden the conflict
Pressure becomes unnecessary once private talks begin

explanation.gentle: The chapter warns that insincere diplomacy does not soften the fight. It makes the channel less believable.
explanation.direct: Watch the failure mode: a decorative exit burns the very leverage it claims to create.
explanation.competitive: A false door teaches the enemy to trust the wall.

questions.prompt: Amina can escalate formally with no private lane, or she can pair escalation with a repair package the vendor could sign. Which fits the chapter best?
choices: The paired move, if the repair package is sincere and usable
The public-only escalation, because pressure should stay pure
Neither, because diplomacy and enforcement should never mix

explanation.gentle: Amina needs both rising cost and believable relief visible at once.
explanation.direct: Apply the dual-track test: escalation works best when the opponent can also see a real end to the escalation.
explanation.competitive: Turn the screw and show the valve.

questions.prompt: Davin is told that paired escalation and settlement are mixed signals. What should he check first?
choices: Whether the pressure track and settlement track point toward the same decision
Whether the other side is emotionally ready to lose
Whether the public message sounds tougher than the private one

explanation.gentle: The signals are not mixed if both tracks make the same exit easier to choose.
explanation.direct: Check alignment, not volume: the strategy works when the shove and the door are coordinated.
explanation.competitive: If both tracks herd them toward one real exit, it is leverage, not noise.

questions.prompt: Yvette has a repair offer ready, but the person receiving it lacks authority to sign it. What does the chapter suggest?
choices: The off-ramp is weaker than it looks because authority is missing
Authority does not matter if the terms are rational
She should intensify pressure and ignore the gap

explanation.gentle: A sincere offer still fails if the recipient cannot actually take it.
explanation.direct: Use the authority test: an exit has to be reachable in practice, not only reasonable on paper.
explanation.competitive: A real door is worthless if the target has no key.

questions.prompt: Cian calls his preferred outcome a compromise, but the other person would have to accept total self-erasure to take it. Which judgment fits the chapter?
choices: It is legitimate diplomatic war because the offer is private
It is a misuse because the off-ramp is disguised surrender
It becomes acceptable if he also applies more pressure

explanation.gentle: The chapter draws a hard line here. A settlement lane has to preserve some real agency and dignity.
explanation.direct: Separate settlement from self-erasure: if acceptance means intolerable collapse of self, the offer is not a real exit.
explanation.competitive: A cardboard door does not stop being fake because you whisper while pointing at it.

questions.prompt: Nerissa sees the public campaign escalating faster than the private terms are improving. What is the best diagnosis?
choices: That is ideal because pressure should always outrun the exit
It proves the other side was never open to agreement
The pressure track may be outrunning the settlement track and risking hardening

explanation.gentle: When the off-ramp loses credibility, the strategy starts decaying into plain escalation.
explanation.direct: Name the imbalance clearly: the squeeze is growing faster than the believable exit, which makes resistance easier to justify.
explanation.competitive: If the door dims while the wall rises, you are breeding entrenchment.

questions.prompt: Where is the ethical line in diplomatic war?
choices: It is crossed whenever pressure and negotiation happen together
It is crossed when the operator borrows the language of settlement while leaving no tolerable or believable way to settle
It is crossed only when the conflict becomes public

explanation.gentle: The chapter allows structured leverage, but not the pretense of agreement without a real path to agree.
explanation.direct: Hold the distinction tightly: a sincere exit preserves agency, while coercive theater only imitates that form.
explanation.competitive: The moral break happens when the door is for optics and the wall is the real offer.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 21 lead into Chapter 22?
choices: It shows that once you negotiate under pressure, you should never stop pressing
It moves from better bargaining leverage to the question of when to stop the campaign before sunk cost takes over
It abandons settlement entirely and returns to annihilation

explanation.gentle: The next chapter asks when even a useful campaign needs an ending.
explanation.direct: Track the transition: Chapter 22 shifts from dual-track leverage to exit judgment and loss acceptance.
explanation.competitive: After forcing terms comes the harder move of knowing when to leave the field.
